speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) gave notice of his intention to raise this matter by way of a question of privilege. I have a dual difficulty here. It seems to me that not only was the hon.

member for Oshawa entitled to say what he said, but so was the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) during the course of the question period. The right hon. Prime Minister may have described the language used by the hon. member for Oshawa as insulting, but that is his right during the question period or at any other time during the proceedings. Similarly, the hon. member for Oshawa said that the particular company to which he made reference during the course of the question period was price-gouging. I do not think that it would be appropriate to enter into a discussion now in defence of either one of the interventions of the two hon. members here this afternoon. 1 will check the record, and if I am wrong in my estimation of the situation, the hon. member shall have leave to raise a question on the matter tomorrow.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to raise a question of privilege, of which I gave you notice last Thursday. I am glad to do so on this day because it is the sixth anniversary in terms of months that this government has held office. My question of privilege deals with the question of openness and the Official Secrets Act. This government has moved further and faster toward openness and honesty than any other government in the last 50 years. But I want to go even further and even faster, and it is for this reason that I raise this particular issue.
On October 18 I moved in the House a motion under Standing Order 43 which the House was good enough to accept. It reads:
That this House recommends that a parliamentary standing or select committee be forthwith given an order of reference to review the terms of the present act, including a study of such recent cases as that of Dr. Peter Treu and The Toronto Sun and to report proposals for suitable changes to the Official Secrets Act, and that no claim of Crown privilege be allowed to limit the extent of inquiry by the committee.
Of course, I refer to the Official Secrets Act. When I raised the point of order last Thursday, it appeared that there was some difficulty between myself and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) as to the terms of the motion which would be brought into this House to implement this particular motion under Standing Order 43.
As 1 understand it, and I think that my hon. friend will accept this, there is some question in the mind of the government as to whether or not this House is competent to pass a
December 4, 1979

motion purporting to authorize one of its committees to make inquiries under any subject matter without regard to the limitations of Crown privilege. Having said that, I make it quite plain that this House and all the members in this House and in the other place are bound by statute law.
It has been suggested in the form advice given to my honourable friend, I believe, that there still exists an indefinable and vague, but possibly still a very strong, practice coming from the days of the royal prerogative that, apart from statutes, members of the government under the bureaucracy may raise on their own initiative without any foundation in statute a question of Crown privilege and can say, "We will not have to give evidence on this issue; we will not have to produce these particular documents". That is the issue. It is a narrow issue but I suggest a very fundamental and important one.
I think it does well to have this House deal with the issue because this government-and I give the government credit for this-is moving toward a situation where the work of this House will be developed to a greater extent through the agency of committees. I think we should know what power those committees will have.
Crown privilege has been defined as the original right in the Crown in ancient days when the king could not be sued to refuse production of documents or discovery of witnesses. It was later extended to members of the Privy Council in the 17th century in order to protect them from charges by giving immunity through non-disclosure of information about their activities. That right has lingered to the present day.
My quarrel with the proposition is that there still exists a non-statutory, superior and royal power in the ranks of the bureaucracy, acting through the ministry, to inhibit a committee of this House from pursuing its inquiries, and that even a unanimous motion of this House is not enough to override this particular principle.
A very good illustration of this is the fact that the House has been debating a motion proposed by the President of the Privy Council which deals with cost overruns. During the course of the investigations by that committee it will probably be essential for members of the committee to ask questions of members of the public service about the ways and means by which these cost overruns were developed. If the proposition of the principle of Crown privilege is to be sustained and put into effect, then I can see that in many instances many members of the public service will say, "We don't intend to answer this question; it may deal with a question of policy or it may deal with a question where the public interest is involved and we don't intend to answer it."
There have been some pretty clear illustrations of this. When the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) was prime minister, he made it perfectly clear that he would not allow the Clerk of the Privy Council to be questioned before a committee. That is an illustration of the use of Crown privilege.
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
In another situation, Mr. Speaker, several years ago the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works was examining Mr. Donald Macdonald who was then minister of energy, mines and resources and whose name is not unknown at the present time. The question arose as to whether certain witnesses who had appeared with Mr. Macdonald could be examined and, if so, the extent of the examination. Mr. Macdonald said, as reported at page 24:32 of the committee proceedings for December 18, 1973, as follows:
This has been a longstanding procedure in the Canadian public service and in the House of Commons that it is a minister who ultimately assumes his responsibility and not individual advisers; I think my position is well founded constitutionally.
On page 24:33 of the proceedings there appears the following exchange between myself and the minister:

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: ... I had the honour to serve as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts for several years, and deputy ministers appeared there by themselves-not under the skirts of the minister. They answered a lot of questions, as did their advisers. When you come to a question of policy, absolutely, a deputy minister or an adviser must defer to the minister; but on questions of fact, deputy ministers and advisers are compellable witnesses to appear here ...

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: I am sorry, that is too much. The minister is responsible; if he chooses to have his deputy minister appear without his being present, that is the minister's choice. But ultimately, it is the minister's responsibility as to who shall appear.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: You do not want us to ...

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: This has been a long-standing parliamentary principle...

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: The minister is wrong. The minister is challenging responsible government, the responsible right of the House of Commons ...

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: 1 must say that responsible government means that a minister is responsible for his portfolio to the House of Commons, not individual public servants.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
The minister would not recognize responsible government if it got into bed with him, that is all I can say.
I suppose that last comment was somewhat improper, Mr. Speaker. These assertions have been made, however. I am glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has indicated that he would have no objection to allowing the Clerk of the Privy Council to appear before a committee. I suggest, however, that it should be as a matter of right, and not a matter of grace. That is the right of this House and this committee, if it sees fit by appropriate action in the House or by direction to its committees.
There has been a lot of discussion on this issue and challenges have been raised in the House and in committee about the subject of judicial decisions. I am not going to take too much of the time of the House because this is a highly academic subject and, more than that, it is a tremendously important one to us. I will, however, touch on the highlights.
The issue was brought up for consideration in the parliament of Australia. In 1975, what was called-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
Order, please. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but while I think I understand the nature of his argument, I do not understand the nature of the problem. The House passed the resolution to which he has made reference and which reads as follows:

December 4, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
That this House recommends that a parliamentary standing or select committee be forthwith given an order of reference to review the terms of the present act, including a study of such recent cases as that of Dr. Peter Treu and The Toronto Sun and to report proposals for suitable changes to the Official Secrets Act, and that no claim of Crown privilege be allowed to limit the extent of inquiry by the committee.
The only basis upon which the hon. member could have a question of privilege, which he is now arguing, is that the House has perhaps disregarded that motion. The motion is not an order. The result of that motion is a resolution recommending "that a parliamentary standing or select committee be forthwith given an order of reference". If the hon. member's complaint is that the House has not moved to give that order of reference, that is an argument that I might want to entertain. He is now saying, however, that there is a difficulty which goes beyond that, but I have not heard it yet from the government.
Perhaps the hon. member could direct his attention to the problem of whether it has been a reasonable time, whether there should be an order and what the terms of the order ought to be. I have not yet heard him say that the House is in default of that order. I would guess that the drafting of the order might be somewhat complex. Perhaps the hon. member could turn his attention to that aspect of the matter.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when you said the "House," I think you meant the government has not complied with that. 1 think that is where the difficulty lies. As I understand it, the government feels that the terms of the order of reference to be given must omit any claim Crown privilege. That is what I take exception to and it is what I think is a question of privilege. I may be wrong in that and if I am 1 will gladly stop now. Maybe my friend the President of the Privy Council has something to say.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext: 1 would want to reserve the right of the hon. member to meet this point. I am not trying to interrupt him to prejudice his argument in any way. He was about to move to establish that part of his argument. It may be appropriate to hear from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) and see whether this argument can be met.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter Baker (President of Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully at the time the hon. member made his motion. Within a day or so after that, 1 sent him a draft of a proposed term of reference with respect to this matter, indicating my own wishes becuse of the emphasis we were placing at that time on freedom of information.
After a reasonable period of time 1 heard from the hon. member that the form of the order was not satisfactory. He also raised the question of Crown privilege. In the meantime, I had received an opinion from the legal officer of the House of Commons that there was some question about the propriety of the matter of Crown privilege.
I then took the unusual step, not just of informing my friend of that, but of sending him a copy of the opinion and asking for his comments on it. I received a letter from him, I believe it
was yesterday, indicating that that was not acceptable to him.
I have not had a chance to reply yet but I can reply now, Mr. Speaker. I am considering the argument he put to me and I think we should comply to the extent that we can within the law.
My concern, Mr. Speaker, is not with respect to the hon. member putting a non-statutory prerogative in the bureaucracy; my problem is with respect to the matter raised by the legal officer of the House of Commons with respect to non-statutory prerogatives in the law.
I think our exchange has been a good one. It was quite a healthy exchange and reasonably expeditious when the exchange finally started. I can undertake to you, sir, to the House and certainly to the hon. member that there is no question of delaying it. I would have no objection whatsoever, having raised the question of privilege today, even though a motion has not been put down and these discussions are continuing, if the matter could be reserved until my law officers look at the material submitted by the hon. member. I undertake to do that quickly. I think the hon. member and the House know that. I will do it quickly and put the reference down. When the reference is down there may be a question of privilege at that point with respect to the terms of the reference.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
That appears to be satisfactory to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
Something occurs to me as well that both hon. members may want to think about, and that is that the resolution that has been adopted by the House recommends that a parliamentary committee be given an order of reference. The concluding sentence is that "no claim of Crown privilege be allowed to limit the extent of inquiry by the committee".
It may be, and 1 would want the hon. members to reflect on this, that the only time a question of privilege can arise then is if during the committee's deliberations that matter of Crown privilege is permitted to limit the extent of the inquiry. I know that the hon. member may want a House order to obviate that possibility, but it may be that an order of reference will in fact comply with all that has been resolved by the House on October 18 and that no offence against that resolution can be considered to have taken place except when the claim of crown privilege is used in the inquiry to limit it. I do not attempt to resolve that point at this time, simply to leave it to the hon. members to consider. Perhaps we can await with dispatch the undertaking of the President of the Privy Council to produce a motion and then see whether or not there is a question of privilege to be taken at that time or at a later time.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be resolved even more rapidly than that; Your Honour makes quite good sense with that comment. It may well be that your order of reference might go as the President of the Privy Council had originally contemplated, but he might at this time consider giving contemporaneously an undertaking that the government will not

December 4, 1979

raise at the time of the committee hearings any non-statutory, government questions of Crown privilege, and we might well then proceed quite expeditiously with the issue.

maintopic: MR. BALDWIN-OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-IMPLEMENTATION OF STANDING ORDER 43 MOTION

While the government tried to insist that it was being the Christmas fairy by handing out goodies to the Canadian people, it became very clear that it was handing out goodies to its own people. A serious omission is that there is no attempt to assist home owners and renters who face the same kind of pressures with regard to housing budgets as do home owners who have mortgages.

were total contradictions. Is the government prepared to provide support for a broader range of Canadians who are feeling the same kind of housing pressures as Canadians who have mortgages?
We listened in debate to the argument that it was the middle class home owner who is the fall guy in the Canadian economy. 1 believe that the Minister of National Revenue and the hon. member for Dauphin said the same thing. I would repeat for the information of the Minister of Finance, because he may have been out of the House at the time or may not have had an opportunity to read the debates, that if he looks at the criterion of need and measures it according to the percentage of budget going toward housing, in every major city across Canada renters face far more severe pressures in their housing budgets than do home owners. For example, in the city of Edmonton 40 per cent of the renters pay over 30 per cent of their budget on rental accommodation as compared to only 17 per cent of home owners. That same ratio is true throughout the country.
We would like the government to clarify its position. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SAFETY OF EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
that Bill C-226, to amend the Canada Labour Code (Safety of Employees), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the private member's bill I am presenting today speaks to one of the most important issues presently facing Canadians and Canadian governments. We have often been led to believe that the most serious question facing labour today is that of collective bargaining and industrial disputes. With all due respect, that is not the most serious question. The most serious issue facing Canadian labour today and, in effect, facing governments at all levels, is the whole question of occupational health and safety in the work place. That is the most burning issue for Canadian labour today.
I am sure members opposite me and those beside me will admit there is a crisis in occupational health and safety. It seems to me that whenever we talk about labour in this country we hear a lot of scapegoating-the Tories are great at that, like the Liberals before them. They start trotting out figures about the number of days lost in strikes, they compare them with figures from Italy, West Germany, Britain, Uganda and every other country in the world. But we never hear much talk about the number of days lost due to accidents on the job or diseases incurred as a result of conditions in the work place, or indeed the whole question of a comparison between days lost and the economic impact on Canada when we consider that the number of days lost due to occupational health problems or accidents on the job was seven times more than days lost through industrial disputes. One can compute the loss in terms of dollars to the Canadian economy.
There is no doubt whatsoever that the previous Liberal government attempted to come to grips with giving the federal government some leadership on the whole question of occupational health and safety when it brought in an amendment to
Canada Labour Code
the Canada Labour Code, Bill C-8, which amended part IV of the Canada Labour Code. In spite of the fact that that was the first amendment to the Canada Labour Code in ten years, it is to the credit of the previous Liberal government that it gave workers the right to refuse work which is unsafe-but only if the danger is imminent, which is hardly adequate since we know that some cancers develop over as long a period as 20 years. That is hardly encouraging when, according to a recent American study, at least 20 per cent of all cancers in the United States are job-related.
The previous Liberal government gave workers the right to health and safety committees, but they were not made mandatory and, in particular, in those areas where there is no collective in the work place there are no health and safety committees. Indeed, the minister has not exercised his right to establish those health and safety committees in those particular situations. He has not exercised his authority to date.
I have here some facts which ought to be put on the record. The federal Department of Labour estimates that 1,071,484 Canadians were injured on the job in 1978. In Ontario alone nearly 1,500 workers died from job-related accidents and illnesses over the last five years. According to a study related to work accidents by Dr. Paul Rohan, a Montreal occupational health and safety specialist, a Canadian worker was disabled on the job every 16 seconds of every day over the past ten years. Another fact I think we should keep in mind is that the frequency of injuries is rising. Over the past ten years the number of employees disabled each year has increased by one-third, and 46 per cent of those who had accidents in 1978 were either temporarily or permanently disabled. Those are the human costs.
There are, of course, monetary costs. Compensation payments for work injuries in 1978 reached $967 million. Those were just compensation payments alone. Counting indirect costs such as production losses, hiring and training of new employees, higher employer insurance costs, overtime and hospital care, the total combined costs arising from work injuries, illnesses and fatalities could be as high as $4 billion a year. Last year, for example, in Ontario alone the workmen's compensation board paid $382,207,000 in compensation awards.
Aside from the fact that the improvements which were made through Bill C-8 to the Canada Labour Code were long overdue, there were some obvious ones which were not made to the Canada Labour Code. We tried to amend Bill C-8. The Liberals would not accept any amendments. Indeed, their concern about this problem is evidenced by the fact that there are only three of them sitting in the House this afternoon. Not one of the previous ministers of labour was prepared to accept changes to the Canada Labour Code which would have corrected the glaring inadequacy of part IV of the Canada Labour Code with which Bill C-226 comes to grips.
The change we wanted and which is in Bill C-226 which we are debating this afternoon is that the provisions of part IV of the Canada Labour Code be extended to those workers under federal jurisdiction who are not already covered under part IV.

December 4, 1979
Canada Labour Code
Part IV makes a neat little exception in eliminating from coverage those who work on trains, boats and planes. When they are on the ground, they are covered by part IV of the code; but once they are on the job in the air, on the running boards of trains or on ships, God help them because there is no coverage whatsoever under part IV of the Canada Labour Code.

They are covered under the Railway Act, and the Railway Act provides no occupational health and safety section. So, for example, those workers who were running that CPR train in Mississauga had no coverage whatsoever with respect to the rights which are in part IV of the Canada Labour Code regarding health and safety. They were not covered at all.
With regard to those people who work on our aeroplanes, once a plane is in the air, stewardesses, pilots, stewards and all the other airline attendants on the plane are not covered. The next time hon. members get on a DC-9, they should take a look at the fold down seat which is located at the back of the plane and in the middle aisle. If a tail cone was to fly off, the workers occupying those places would be sucked right out the back. There is no coverage under the Aeronautics Act with respect to health and safety. The same thing goes for those who work on ships.
The unions representing workers in these areas have been after governments for over ten years, and they have always listened. There have been labour ministers galore. They have listened. No one can accuse them of not listening, but they do not act. The present minister is not listening. He is busy carrying on his own private little conversation. He is Mr. Nice Guy. speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Wightman (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SAFETY OF EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill put forward by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is of particular interest to me and he is to be commended for it because, inadvertently or not, it raises, among other things, an issue which is very close to the heart of this government. The issue 1 refer to is regulatory reform.
One effect of this bill would be to simplify and rationalize many of the regulations pursuant to occupational safety which are now to be found in a variety of pieces of legislation covering public employees, employees in both the public and private sectors in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, as well as all the people who are now covered by part IV of the Canada Labour Code. Bill C-226, as 1 said, would be a device whereby that legislation could be simplified, and to that extent it is consistent with the preoccupation of this government to clear away a good deal of the underbrush and to look very hard at the proliferation of regulations which are now in place.
During the course of this summer 1 had cause to have delivered to my office copies of the consolidated code of Canada, all 18 volumes. A law student ten or 12 years ago would not even be concerned about the consolidated regulations; they would have been encompassed in one small volume. But today they amount to some 18 volumes, and that is only regulations which have been codified; it does not speak to the plethora of regulations that come about as the result of quasi-judicial bodies of all sorts. So we should all be grateful that the hon. member for Nickel Belt has raised the issue in this fashion.
What is relevant on this matter of over-regulation is the cost to society of keeping these regulations in place. Bill C-226 could be one of the ways of moving toward less regulation,
Canada Labour Code
both as the regulations exist now or as they might come into place in the future.
Another approach to regulatory reform can be seen in the work that has been going on between the provincial and federal governments in terms of attempting to reduce the overlap of administration. Our government, and in particular, our Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), has been profoundly interested in this exercise and in support of it. We acknowledge the efforts of the previous administration to develop a socioeconomic impact analysis as a means of testing the efficacy of the particular new major health, safety and fairness regulations. We have supported that and we have added to the administrative guidelines to ensure that that type of program will become operative. 1 suggest that it is a pioneering step in the regulatory process, the importance of which we as a government hope will be fully recognized by Canadians.
As you know, sir, the notion is that each proposal for new social legislation, if its estimated cost is in the order of $10 million or more, must now be subjected to a formal cost-benefit analysis. The result of that is to be published in the Canada Gazette for the purpose of receiving comments 60 days before the regulation is to take effect. Anyone who could be potentially affected by those regulations is invited to comment to the sponsoring department. As I said, we feel that that is a pioneering step and I am grateful that the hon. member for Nickel Belt has today brought this to the attention of the House.
The hon. member has given an indication as to who would be affected by this proposal, and I think that perhaps for purposes of completeness of the debate we should take a look at precisely who would be affected. In the federal jurisdiction there are nine principal federal departments or agencies administering 16 separate acts which are concerned in varying degrees with occupational safety and health. They include the Department of Labour, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. As 1 have said earlier, were we to proceed with the bill at hand, a good deal of these numbers would be reduced.
However, 1 am sure the hon. member did not intend to lead people to believe that people working on trains, ships and aircraft are totally unprotected, which of course is not the case. His words, I believe, were, "God help them when they step on the running boards of the trains".

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SAFETY OF EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as 1 was pointing out, we have a whole body of arbitration case law, and at no time am I aware of a decision going against an employee who had a genuine apprehension of bodily harm or of injury and having refused to perform or carry out an assignment. Indeed, it goes beyond that, beyond an apprehension of injury to himself or to other workers or, indeed, if he was requested to do something that would be self-denigrating in any way. 1 know of no decision that has not gone with the employee.
Even in the absence of the protection that is offered by the various pieces of legislation covering these other employees who are not now embraced by part IV of the Canada Labour Code, I know of no such decision.
It might be useful for the purposes of this discussion to adumbrate the departments or agencies and the legislation which obtains in respect of employees of those departments and agencies. The Ministry of Transport employees come under the Aeronautics Act as well as the Canada Shipping Act. The Canadian Transport Commission comes under the Railway Act. The Atomic Energy Control Board comes under the Atomic Energy Control Act. Energy, Mines and Resources and Indian and Northern Affairs come under the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, and the National Energy Board comes under the National Energy Board Act. The Department of Labour, of course, comes under the Canada Labour Code.
There are a few points in respect of Bill C-226 that 1 would suggest should be considered here before any consideration be given to moving the bill onward to the committee. We should consider, for instance, the question of territorial exclusion. Since the bill would remove territorial exclusion, it seems to me we have to look at that rather seriously, because that exclusion which is provided for in subsection 81 of the Canada Labour Code would need to be retained if the member's bill were to go forward. To take that right to regulate works and undertakings or businesses of a local or private nature away from the governments of the Yukon Territory and of the Northwest Territories, would certainly be an unwarranted and regressive action in the development of territorial government. Perhaps Bill C-226 could be refined to that extent.
In respect of public service employees, it seems to me, with the Treasury Board acting as employer, the government in an August, 1968, directive affirmed a policy of applying the principles of the Canada Labour Safety Code and the regulations and standards adopted thereunder to the public service. The portion of the proposal that would make departmental corporations subject to the Canada Labour Code has merit,

but a case has not been fully developed at this time to suggest that employees in the federal public service do not have protection equivalent to that of workers covered by the Canada Labour Code, part IV.
Finally, sir, let me say a word regarding international treaties and obligations. Canada is respectful of its international treaties and obligations, if some countries are not, and we do have international laws and agreements relating to the operation of ships and aircraft. They, as well as the overriding concern for passenger safety, can take precedence over the safety of employee provisions in part IV of the Canada Labour Code. Bill C-226 would remove the order in council provision of section 80(2) which is required to prevent any conflict between our international treaty obligations and our own laws. I would not think the bill should go forward without that imperfection having been cured.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SAFETY OF EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
1 think we must, on all sides of this House, and the hon. member has suggested this, agree on the importance of the issue he has attempted to address, that of lost time due to occupational health problems and accidents. We are conscious of this, not simply as to the economic implications but, most particularly, as to the human implications and the human suffering that are implied.
At the same time 1 think it is the hon. member who attempts to relate occupational safety and health problems with industrial disputes. The two are almost mutually exclusive; at least they are not comparable in terms of an indication as to the state of labour-management relations in Canada or the health of labour-management relations.
There are real distinctions between a work stoppage where everybody goes out on the same day or at the same time, and the type of lost time that is implied in accident or health problems. They do not normally all occur on the same day. In that sense those two reasons for lost time really do not bear comparison.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 think we should be mindful of this reality. There are jobs performed by people which implicitly are dangerous. A policeman's job is dangerous, and a fireman's job is dangerous. The nature of that work is such that the public interest must and does come first. Of course those good people would have it no other way.
We have before us a proposal which 1 think draws this fact very much to our attention. Consider, sir, the responsibilities of flight crews and flight attendants vis-a-vis the passengers. Whether because of a malfunction of the aircraft, or because of some terrorist taking over the aircraft, the responsibility of those attendants and pilots, and their first concern, must be for
December 4, 1979

passenger safety, even though it is at the expense of those workers themselves.
I think of the recent disaster at Mississauga. Although the precise causes of the mishap are not known as yet, envisage a situation where a locomotive engineer sees an imminent problem and is capable of doing something about it, but in staying with the train he places himself in some jeopardy. I do not think we can have legislation which would suggest that, if it comes to a choice between his own safety and the safety of perhaps thousands of other passengers on that train, his responsibility is unclear.
One could easily conjure up any number of situations and occupations wherein the public interest and safety are of paramount concern. We should be grateful to the hon. member for introducing this bill in this way because, as I said, it does raise this important issue and exemplifies the problems there are in trying to solve all problems through legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I would hope that at some appropriate time the hon. member opposite would withdraw the word "deliberate". I am not sure that it fits into the traditions of this House.
I think the hon. member confirms the major thesis that 1 was attempting to develop. He has an objective; he wants to protect the health of all employees on airplanes, on ships, and on railroads. He has to ask himself, however, whether the
amendment he proposes in this bill accomplishes that end. That is the relationship between motivation and fact.
I would ask the hon. member if there is not a way of addressing this problem that would be more specific to the problem and more appropriate to the problem, without confusing the universe. I suggest that the exclusions presently contained in the Canada Labour Code are there for specific reasons. The specific reasons in these three areas of human endeavour are the peculiarities of them. If hon. members on that side of the House really care about the health and safety of employees in those three industries, why do they not come forward with a private member's bill or an amendment in committee that would protect the health and safety of both members of the general public and employees at the same time? Instead, they try to bicycle through the kind of provision which does not allow for the attention to detail which should be relevant to a specific industry.
1 do not want to go on at length, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to make one last point. I believe it was the deliberate intent of previous legislators to exclude people in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. What the hon. member proposes is another example of what we have seen too often in this country-the continuation of a kind of paternalism.
I believe that people who work in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon have the right and the obligation to set forth labour codes and labour standards that cover their experience in the north which, too frequently, is not the same as that in the south. The north has 24-hour days and 24-hour nights. The legislation should be specific to their circumstances. Any attempt to bicycle this through on top of existing legislation should be defeated by the House.

Mr. Speaker, 1 really do not want to speak on the point of order raised by the hon. member, because it would take up the three or four minutes that are left, and I know that would upset him.
Certainly, as legislators we must always be concerned with how changes in legislation or, indeed, new legislation will affect the safety of those who have to carry out the policy. Therefore, there is much merit in a proposal like Bill C-226. The concern for the safety of employees is important and should never be neglected. The hon. member is well aware of that, and points it out at every opportunity. However, 1 feel that this amendment to the Canada Labour Code will create some legal problems or situations and, while it tries to solve others, on balance it will do little to clear up the whole situation.
As 1 said, the safety of employees working in the federal government, or indeed in the private sector, should not be taken lightly. I am surprised that the hon. member for Nickel Belt did not mention that the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety is to be located in the great thriving metropolis of Hamilton. This centre can, and will, do much to look into problems of occupational safety and, in the long run, 1 am sure will do much to make the work place safer.
It is through activities co-ordinated at the national level that solutions will be found to problems which the hon. member for Nickel Belt obviously knows exist, and which are a potential danger to those workers not included in the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.
The workers excluded from part IV of the Canada Labour Code are protected by other federal statutes, as the hon. member knows. The question is not whether workers should be protected by federal statutes but, rather, by which statutes. I take this opportunity to speak on the matter with a real sense of commitment and concern, Mr. Speaker, the same commitment and concern with which 1 judge the hon. member and Bill C-226. The present situation is that these workers are protected by the Treasury Board. This protection is similar to the provisions of part IV of the Canada Labour Code and its regulations.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments I would like to make on Bill C-20, and then a couple of brief questions for the minister.
There have been repeated references made all through the debate by the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party to try to give the distinct impression that there are absolutely no plans at all to assist renters federally or provincially, and absolutely no other pieces of legislation to assist home owners in any way at all. Of course, this is just absolute nonsense.
There has also been reference to the fact that tax forms are printed. I think there has hardly been a year go by in the seven
Mortgage Tax Credit
years 1 have been here that there have not been tax forms printed in advance of the passing of a piece of legislation, so 1 do not know what all the hullabaloo about that is for. There is nothing new about that at all.
I have just done some research on the number of housing assistance programs there are in Canada. 1 have done it for a couple of provinces and federally, and the number of programs there are to assist renters now is amazing. We have the federal government program, non-profit co-operatives, and in that particular piece of assistance there is a section dealing with renters which says:
Additionally, for income assisted units, assistance will be provided to reduce occupancy charges to levels as determined by the rent to income scale.
It goes into detail on how it assists renters.
Here is another one: provincial and municipal housing. In this particular assistance program there is a section on renting.
It says:
-encourage the application of provincial assistance in order to penetrate further down the income range and provide rental assistance to those individuals and families who need it most-
This particular program goes on. It has another section on rents and the assistance that groups are getting with regard to rent assistance now.
Then there is another one, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. It is to assist landlords in selected municipalities who agree to rent controls and non-profit corporations and co-operatives.
Then there is another one: insured loans for rental housing. It goes into a lot of detail on how it gives assistance to renters.
I find it very strange that this knowledgeable opposition has not read any of this into the record. Instead, we have their usual tricks of misleading the Canadian people that there are not any other programs at all to assist renters or home owners, federally or provincially.
Then we have the public assistance housing program which is in effect. It has a section on renters, rent supplements.
The provinces enter into agreements with non-profit housing corporations, housing co-operatives and private owners of rental properties to subsidize the rents of low-income tenants-
It goes on to explain. Then there is another one, private non-profit housing corporations, rental policy: .
Tenants will pay a reasonable portion of their income in rent up to the market rent.
Then it goes into detail on how another group is being assisted with rent assistance.
Then there is another one, graduated payment mortgages for new rental properties. It goes into detail to explain how that is helping renters. The legislation is all there. Why have the Liberals not told people about it, instead of trying to mislead them that there are no programs at all to assist anybody at all? Do hon. members think this is the first piece of housing legislation to assist home owners which has ever been brought into this country?

December 4, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
There are others. There is a summary of National Housing Act programs. It goes on and on into great detail about assistance to home owners, renters, and everybody else. Actually the renters have assistance now in one way, along with many others. It is because mortgage interest and property taxes are a deductible business expense for landlords, and renters are already receiving similar benefits. Also, Bill C-20 has some spinoff benefits for renters. As more Canadians, encouraged by our tax credits, move into their own homes, more rental accommodation will become available, thus taking pressure off those who choose to continue to rent.
It is impossible to meet the needs of all Canadians with one government program. 1 should like anybody in this House to get up and tell me of one piece of legislation that has been brought in that is going to assist the whole country, or every home owner or every renter. No such piece of legislation has ever been introduced in any country since day one.
I	do not have the statistics for all the ten provinces and two territories, but I have quite a bit for Manitoba and Ontario on the way they are assisting the renters. In Manitoba, recognizing that rising rents, coupled with fixed incomes, put terror into the hearts of Manitoba senior citizens, the provincial Conservative government has wisely designed a new rent subsidy program which will help 9,000 elderly for the relatively low price of $3.5 million.
There is another program. In Manitoba we have rent controls, and here are all the details on how they are protecting renters. There are about 12 different steps in the legislation that protects renters in Manitoba, and here is a list of just a few of the programs that are in place in Ontario designed for renters. There is the private assistance rental program, the general public housing assistance program, the public housing municipal sponsors, the public housing provincial sponsors, the federal-provincial senior citizens rural housing program, the federal and municipal non-profit housing program, and the rent supplement program. On and on it goes with programs to help people, and Bill C-20 is just another step to give more assistance. I do not know why there is so much objection to assisting another group.
Recently the Ontario government announced a $2 million project. Community agencies will propose projects which will be funded 50-50 by themselves and the provincial government. The agencies can raise money by fees, fund raising, or municipal support. Projects will be aimed at providing services which will allow senior citizens to remain in their own homes. There is also a program in Manitoba to assist senior citizens to stay in their own homes.
The total spending in Ontario for 1979 is $60 million, and in Toronto it is estimated that $1,055,000 will be spent on four major projects. The federal government shares in about $2,110,000 which is a joint program to assist home owners, renters and all the rest. Toronto has a neighbourhood development program costing $650,000, and the federal funding reaches $1,300,000. So we are certainly spending millions and

millions from the federal budget, along with Bill C-20. Also, Toronto has a downtown revitalization program totalling $12,300,000, and so does Winnipeg, and so does Montreal have a program to revitalize their older areas.
Here is further Manitoba support in housing, Mr. Chairman. The government provides more than 75 per cent of all senior citizens with relief from 100 per cent of school taxes on their homes, and 75 per cent of all pensioners or tenants receive property tax credits sufficient to offset a portion of their taxes contributable to school taxes under the new pensioner school taxes assistance program. There have been major improvements in the critical home repair program. Also, the Manitoba government has introduced the shelter allowance for elderly residents which provides subsidies directly for people in need. This year the Manitoba government will spend $120 million on financial assistance to senior citizens. I suppose that if the Liberals had not banged up the country, there would be more money to hand out. But we have to pay off the Liberals' debts first before we can introduce any more programs or expand on them.
1	have two brief questions for the minister, Mr. Chairman. I should like to ask him if the community services program has gone into effect. This is an additional program which, I understand, started in 1979 with a funding level of $150 million. As of January 1, 1980, it is supposed to increase to $250 million. 1 should like to ask the minister if contracts for that program have been signed and whether it is going into effect in 1980.

heating fuel, 1 wonder if the Minister of Finance and the government should not have taken steps to cushion such an exorbitant cost increase. The Minister of National Elealth and Welfare talks of reviewing social programs, family allowances, old age security, help to the handicapped. He has been refusing since this session started to put forward the kind of bill that has been urged by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on the special allowance to increase the pensions paid to our veterans' widows.

The Minister of Finance talks of a deficit reduction, cost reductions in many departments, a 60,000 reduction in the size of the public service, and even elimination or curtailment of certain departmental services.
I wonder if, in order to act wisely and consistently, the government and the Minister of Finance should not have looked for fairer alternatives to help a much greater number of Canadians who are suffering under present economic conditions.
There is also a matter of principle 1 must raise for myself and some of my colleagues. I dealt with this last Wednesday, on pages 1812-1813 of Hansard, and I have no intention of repeating my remarks. However, this concerned regional disparities, and 1 would like to quote from that speech. Even if there is repetition I think this could help the minister:

Because the credit does not apply to those who have paid off their mortgages on the homes they own, as well as to renters, the benefits of the program are even more unevenly distributed. In Newfoundland, for example, 82 per cent of home owners do not have mortgages. In British Columbia the figure is 43 per cent. In Ontario it is 43 per cent, and in Quebec it is 41 per cent. We can therefore see that Newfoundlanders will be benefiting little while still sharing the cost.
The results are that the Atlantic region loses out because of the high percentage of people who own homes without mortgages, 70 per cent, and Quebec loses out because of the high percentage of renters, which is 49 per cent. Yet these are two of the areas which are in most need of housing assistance.
The mortgage interest tax credit program is so unevenly distibuted that of the four provinces we have examined, Ontario, which has 36 per cent of Canada's population and 37 per cent of the nation's home owners, will receive 45 per cent of the benefits of the program. British Columbia with 11 per cent of Canada's population and 12 per cent of the nation's home owners will receive 16 per cent of the benefits. Newfoundland with 2.4 per cent of Canada's population and 2.4 per cent of the country's home owners will receive only 1.2 per cent of the benefits. Quebec with fully 27 per cent of Canada's population and 22 per cent of Canada's home owners will receive only 19 per cent of the benefits.
We believe in the redistribution of wealth, but redistribution to alleviate disparity, not to add to it. The unfair redistribution of this tax credit will create more regional disparity.

The purpose and the object of the Canadian constitution are the elimination of regional disparities but, instead of eliminating them, this program increases them.

Mr. Chairman, there is another question I wish to raise concerning this bill, that of alterations. As I said earlier, in normal circumstances, in an economy where we might afford a certain luxury, a bill like this one might be acceptable, but as the Minister of Finance said himself, our present financial situation does not allow us to help everybody. But I wish to say that the allocation of a tax credit in respect of a mortgage secured to finance alterations is perfectly unrealistic. You must make repairs costing not less than $5,000 to be eligible. The large majority of home owners undertake repairs that cost much less. 1 would ask the Minister of Finance, why not reduce that minimum to $1,000 or $2,000? Why not improve home rehabilitation programs and allocate them more funds? That money would be used for much more useful purposes.
This bill, Mr. Chairman, will not encourage a general rehabilitation of homes and will not allow most people to improve their present home instead of being forced to buy another one. If the minister agreed to reduce the minimum from $5,000 to $1,000, maybe he could at least take credit for a bill which would stimulate urban renovation in some areas and that would obviously help people who really need it rather than those who have to make repairs costing at least $5,000.

Throughout the seventies, Mr. Chairman, the Liberal government promoted the supply aspect of housing. In many areas there is now even an oversupply of housing. As well as affordability, quality is one of the important concerns for the 1980s. Renovation and rehabilitation are needed in many homes, not only to improve the quality of housing but to increase the energy efficiency of our accommodation across the land. This means an emphasis on social housing programs and an improvement of substandard units.
I would have much preferred a bill which included and covered the quality of the neighbourhood communities, provided more resources to improve our existing programs, residential rehabilitation assistance, neighbourhood improvement, older home insulation assistance and assistance for the development of co-operative, non-profit and public housing. We must improve housing codes and standards across Canada. We must help Canadians who have acute housing problems-the elderly, the single parent families, the underprivileged, and our native people.
To realize these objectives this tax credit proposal is not an appropriate tool. Anyone who believes that it will do anything concrete to help people to buy homes, when the government creates an economic atmosphere in which purchasing a house is a bad investment, is dreaming. I have given the reasons why I voted against this bill, and I think that they are pretty damned good ones.

The opposition says, "Come on!" Let us have a look at all the people who will benefit from this program. It has long been established that the young of this country want to own homes. This is going to help them buy their homes. It will reduce the income level required for young Canadians who want to buy a home, and it will ease the burden once they have reached that goal.
Mortgage Tax Credit
I am sure hon. members opposite have elderly people as well as young people in their ridings and I would ask them to remember that. This is going to help the elderly remain in their homes. Unfortunately, sometimes the elderly are forced to leave their homes because of high property taxes, but this will help ease that burden.
The benefit to middle-class Canadians will be relief from the ever-rising costs, whether or not they have mortgages. Renters will benefit because the program will make it easier for them to buy homes, and this in turn will ease pressure on the rental market. In the area of Vancouver which I represent, the vacancy rate for rental property is less than one per cent. This has come about largely as a result of the policies of the former government which discouraged investment in rental housing. While I do not think this program will lower rents, it will help stabilize them for people who wish to continue as tenants.
The program will also have benefits for the poor, Mr. Speaker. Any clever tax adviser in this country could counsel people with any means at all, so that all of the interest paid on a mortgage is tax deductible. This program will allow the so-called poor in the country the same benefit of deducting mortgage interest that has been enjoyed for so many years by those who are well off. Members of the NDP want to know how that can come about. 1 do not know whether, in their ridings, there are not any young people who are having trouble with mortgages, or any poor people having trouble hanging on to their homes. The program will help the people the NDP claims to champion, by putting them on the same basis as that enjoyed for many years by people with means.
The program will also help the unemployed as it will create a lot of jobs in the housing sector. The minister covered that area quite extensively when he spoke.
The opposition has objected that there is no assistance to renters in the program. Mr. Chairman, all Canadians are renters or home owners, so the obvious, implied, suggestion of the opposition is that taxpayers should be given an over-all tax cut. It is equally obvious that the government is in no position to make an over-all tax cut to all Canadians. Earlier the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said that this was not a housing measure, but a taxation measure. Mr. Chairman, the government has never claimed that it is anything but an economic measure. If it were a social measure we would bring in a general tax cut or help the poor in some other way. This, Mr. Chairman, is a stimulative measure. It will allow those who can afford to stimulate the economy to do so, with a little help from the government. It was never intended as a social measure. It is an economic measure designed to stimulate the housing industry. It will solve the problem of something like 17 per cent unemployment in the housing industry. It is also a very effective way to assist the housing industry.
I would ask hon. members to compare the experience in this country with that of the United States. I had occasion to visit the United States, in company with the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood and the hon. member for Westmount, to examine the myriad of programs for aid to housing that

exist there. We found that housing administrators were the greatest fans of their own programs. Officials in Washington readily admitted that the so-called middle class was unable to afford the very type of housing that they were being taxed to provide, a kind of first-class housing for the so-called poor. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the cost of those housing programs was so high, taxation was so high, and the result was such that those paying the bulk of the taxes to provide this type of housing in the United States could not afford that very housing themselves.
It is true, as 1 am sure hon. members opposite will remind the House, that the officials we met in Washington advised, "Don't do it." They gave all kinds of reasons why Canada should not adopt such a program, but essentially it was that once you get into it, you cannot get out of it. Every official who criticized this kind of program, however, admitted that he himself had benefited very nicely from such a program, and all of them said that it helped not only themselves with their particular housing problems but that it helped the housing industry in that country. Of course, in advising Canada not to get into this kind of taxation scheme, the officials who run the programs in the United States were defending their own self-interest. It became very evident that they really liked running their programs, extensive as they were, and that the more expensive and elaborate the programs were, the more of them they had, the better the bureaucrats liked it.
1 ask the committee to compare that kind of scheme with the one being offered by the Minister of Finance. This program could be very easily administered through the income tax department. There would be few, if any, additional costs, and the revenues would be directed into the industry, with all of the attendant benefits.
It is interesting to note that in the United States all interest, not only mortgage interest but interest on consumer purchases and even state taxes, has been deductible since 1913. We were told that some 50 per cent of home owners do not have a mortgage and that home owners are given a $3,200 global tax exemption. Of the 50 per cent of ail Americans who own homes and have mortgages, only 25 per cent, in other words, half of those who have mortgages, claimed more than the $3,200 global tax exemption. The resultant loss to the treasury is much less than is even contemplated by this government. With only 25 per cent of taxpayers making the claim in the United States, I think we can expect the same kind of progression in this country and so the loss will be much less than has been anticipated. The program will not be a great tax drain but, instead, will be a boon to all Canadians.
I hope hon. members opposite will take the trouble to talk to their constituents about this. They would then realize that members of whatever age and whatever style of living, of whatever party, of whatever wealth, are interested in this kind of measure because it is a simply administered, beneficial to the econony, kind of measure.

In particular, to my friends in the official opposition I suggest that they compare notes with the new member from Vancouver Centre who, I might observe, is the only member of their party west of Winnipeg. Ask that member from Vancouver Centre about the questionnaire he sent out to his electors. It will be worth observing that Vancouver Centre contains what is known as the west end of Vancouver. It has a density of about 50,000 people per square mile. 1 believe that area has the highest population density in Canada and the second highest population density in North America. The member for Vancouver Centre asked his electors if they favoured mortgage interest deductibility, the program being offered by our Progressive Conservative government. His electors voted 60 per cent in favour of that program. I appeal to members opposite to recall that their electors are no different from those electors in Vancouver Centre who may be tenants but who want to become home owners, and who see this program as a great boon to their future.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this evening I want to speak in relation to clause 1 of Bill C-20. A look at the clause helps confirm how far Bill C-20 is from the original Conservative promise of mortgage interest and property tax deductibility. The one promise the Conservatives had been saying they were going to keep was allowing the deductibility of mortgage interest and property taxes from income for tax purposes. In spite of strong arguments against the soundness of any such scheme that were made over the past year or so, there were those among the public who continued to believe it responded to a need which they wanted government to deal with through the tax system. It has been my belief that there could be an approach to the cost of housing, to the cost of shelter for Canadians, which would be different from that of the Conservatives in being fairer and less costly to them as taxpayers than the Conservative proposal.
Last September the Minister of Finance in effect admitted that the Liberals were right when they criticized the original Conservative mortgage interest deductibility scheme on the grounds of complexity and on the grounds that it was unfair to lower and middle-income Canadians. The minister then said he was abandoning his original scheme for one permitting a credit of a certain proportion of mortgage interest and property taxes against the personal income tax payable by home owners. To use the minister's own words spoken at his press conference last September, he said:
A tax credit is used because it is both simpler and fairer than a deduction . .. it gives greater benefits to lower income and middle-income Canadians.
This is exactly what the Liberals said in criticizing the original proposal.
Before and during the election the Conservatives argued that they knew what they were doing when they proposed their scheme of allowing deductions of a certain amount of mortgage interest and property tax from incomes for tax purposes. But last September 18, and later in presenting bill C-18 to the House, the Minister of Finance in effect confirms that he and
December 4, 1979

his party did not really know what they were doing when they made their original promise. This change, this flip-flop, should undermine most of what little credibility the Conservatives may still have had left with those Canadian voters who were impressed with the scheme in its initial form as presented during the election.
While the Conservative scheme as set out in Bill C-20 is an improvement on the original one, it still has a number of serious flaws, a number of serious gaps, as has been pointed out by many on this side of the House. Bill C-20 does nothing for the large number of Canadians who rent. It does nothing, except for a limited credit for property tax, for the large numbers of home owners who have no mortgages on their homes. It does nothing for home owners whose incomes are too low for them to be required to pay income tax. These people get nothing from Bill C-20.
There is another great flaw in the Conservative approach, that is, the failure of the Minister of Finance to say where the money for the proposal in Bill C-20 will come from. Today the minister went on at great length in trying to explain that options, variations, on the proposal in Bill C-20 that would help groups not covered by it, could not be brought in by his government at this time. He argued all of these options would be too expensive, and therefore he and the Conservative government could not implement them. He said his government was not out for popularity though they were a minority. They had to be responsible, he said, and concerned about the size of the deficit, $11 billion, but a deficit he has admitted was less than the Liberals had forecast when they presented their budget in November, 1978.
The minister was so busy wiping away his crocodile tears about all this that he never bothered to tell us why he was not worried about the almost $3 billion cost of Bill C-20 in its fourth year of operation, and the more than $500 million cost this year, and about how all this would expand the deficit he apparently is also claiming to be so worried about. He claimed speed in passing the bill is necessary so people eligible for it can fill in the tax forms his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, so conveniently sent out even before the bill was passed.
It seems to me that the real reason for the minister's desire for speedy passage of this bill by the House is so that he would not have to explain where the money to pay for it is coming from. This is something he would have to do if this bill were part of a budget, or if final decisions on it were not taken until after his budget was presented.
One initiative pledged by the Conservatives as a way of improving the federal government's fiscal management was to present a budget which brought together and described not only all government expenditures through payments to individuals and companies and in transfers to provinces, but also its tax expenditures. These are the revenues it forgoes when it provides a vast range of allowances, deductions, credits, exemptions and so on to both individuals and business. 1 want to say this would be a desirable initiative. It has been the manner of presenting budgets in the United States, Britain and
Mortgage Tax Credit
West Germany for some years. It reflects a valid idea that a government should present a complete and accurate picture of all forms of its expenditure and how these are being paid for, and by whom.
The President of the Treasury Board spoke of the government's intentions in this regard when he took part in the throne speech debate. In my view this concept already has been undermined, if not totally destroyed, to say the least by the way the government has gone about trying to implement this mortgage interest and property tax credit proposal. Bill C-20 involves a major new program requiring substantial amendment to the income tax law, starting with this clause 1 which we are debating right now, and affecting substantially the balance of government revenue and expenditures. But the Minister of Finance has not presented it as part of a budget. It has been brought in as a separate bill in advance of and separate from his budget. As I have said, the Conservatives are justifying this method on the grounds that speed is necessary if the bill is to become law so that the credit can be claimed by those eligible as part of the completion of their 1979 tax forms. It also means that by presenting it before the budget, the Minister of Finance is obviously hoping to get it passed without having to say how the plan will be paid for.
In fact, in his speech opening debate on second reading of the bill, he was reluctant to admit that the program involved a substantial tax expenditure for which the government would have to find the money. He admitted that the plan would cost $579 million in its first year of operation, and over $2 billion, close to $3 billion, in its fourth year. But all he said about how it would be paid for was that the money would be found in people's pockets; those who would get this new credit.
But this is $2 billion, almost $3 billion, the government would otherwise have collected in tax revenues, revenues it was spending on government programs, including payments to individuals and companies, and in transfers to provinces. The government will have to find that money, either through borrowing to increase its deficit, cutting down substantially on its existing programs, raising taxes, or some combination of all three. But this Conservative government is now pledging not only that it will not increase the deficit but, instead, that it will actually reduce it.
The government has not said what programs now providing useful service to the public it would cut out or reduce. However, the only way it could pay for a program the size and cost of the tax credit plan would be through some pretty massive cuts in existing programs, including programs that those who would be receiving the tax credit plan would likely consider necessary and desirable. Such cuts could well cancel out, eliminate, benefits from the tax credit plan for these people, assuming any benefits are left after the impact of the Conservative high interest rates. The burden of the elimination of programs would also fall on the many Canadians who will not benefit from this plan-the renters, those who do not have

December 4, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
mortgages on their homes, and those whose incomes are too low to pay enough tax to qualify for the tax credit.
One hint as to how the Conservatives intend to pay for the plan may be found in the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has pledged that the existing family allowance program and income tax deductions for children would remain in their present form only during 1979 and 1980. But one should ask why the money for the tax expenditure involved in the mortgage tax program should come only from cuts in social welfare programs for families, or in federal programs providing direct services like health and safety inspections to the public, rather than from cuts in other tax expenditure programs, for example, some of those available to the large multinational oil companies.
If the cost of this mortgage tax plan is to come from higher taxes, which ones will be increased, and by how much? The minister has not been willing to say. There is a hint in the Prime Minister's statement to the first ministers' conference on oil pricing two weeks ago. In it he spoke of his government's desire to impose an energy self-sufficiency tax on higher revenues going to oil companies as a result of the rapid increase to world prices he was promoting.
He also spoke of wanting a sizeable increase in the excise tax on gasoline. But while he talked of using the proceeds for the purpose of moving to energy self-sufficiency, a closer reading of his speech shows he was not saying all the yield from these new taxes would be used in this way. For example, he spoke of the yield of the energy self-sufficiency tax being used for energy related projects. This means it could be used to pay for the oil import compensation fund making up the difference between the high price of imported oil and the Canadian price. In turn this means that $700 million now being spent by the government for this could be used for other purposes, including the first year's cost of the tax credit plan. Also, as I have pointed out, the Prime Minister has said that this tax would yield in excess of $5 billion in additional revenue.
A lot more money would be there as well for that kind of objective from the higher excise tax on gasoline for which he is pushing. The Prime Minister was careful to say all of this would not go into his proposed energy project investment fund. So these high taxes, proposed as part of his new energy package, could in large part be a disguised way of getting all Canadians to pay for the mortgage tax credit plan, including those not benefiting from it at all, and helping offset any benefit even for those eligible for it.
Originally the Conservatives, before they were elected, suggested a substantial portion of the plan would be paid for by higher tax revenue coming from government activity in the building industry, as a result of a stimulus provided by the mortgage interest proposal. This is now most unlikely because of the increases in interest rates since June of this year. At best the mortgage interest plan will help maintain activity at some point near current levels, counteracting the damaging effect of the record high interest rates on the home building and construction industry. The reductions in mortgage rates announced recently by some financial institutions, but to what

are still record high levels, demonstrate the damage the Conservative high interest rate policy has been doing to the construction industry. Some mortgage rates have dropped slightly because people are simply not applying for mortgages to be used for home building and construction.
The Conservatives promised home owners with mortgages, and prospective home owners, they would be better off because of the Conservative mortgage interest proposal than they were before it was promised. This will now not be true because of the Conservative high interest rates policy. It is actually cancelling out benefits for those who had hoped to gain from it. At best, they will be the same as they were before the plan and before the mortgage increases last June. Some will be worse off even with the tax credits.
Any benefits from this plan will also be offset by the higher costs of home heating from the Conservative proposal for increases in energy prices.
The minister said if members were genuinely concerned with high interest rates that the bill would be passed quickly. If this is his argument, he should want to limit the bill's application initially to one year. If he does not agree to this he is saying, in effect, these Conservative high interest rates will be going on forever, or at least while the Conservatives remain in office.
The minister also had the nerve to say the $2 billion cost of this plan means the Conservatives are carrying out their promise of a $2 billion tax cut. Let us get back to what they actually said. There were promises both of a mortgage interest plan and a separate $2 billion cut in personal income tax, a promise the Prime Minister has already confirmed has been abandoned.
The manner in which the government is presenting its mortgage interest plan to Parliament means members are being asked to vote on it by the Conservatives without either they, or the Canadian people, knowing where the cost will come from, who will bear the burden, and whether as a result the plan is justified in light of that burden.
This House needs some answers and the Canadian people need some answers before any final decision can be taken by the House on this bill. I, and members of the official opposition. recognize that there is a problem to be dealt with. The cost of shelter has been rising faster than disposable income, and faster than the cost of living. What is needed is a fair and effective program to deal with this general and basic problem, one which affects renters and people who own homes without mortgages, as well as those who do not have enough income to be liable for income tax against which a credit can be claimed.
The Liberal amendments set forth by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry in his speech on second reading contain the elements of such a program, one that would be fairer and more effective and have a lesser cost for taxpayers than the cost of this Bill C-20. If the Conservatives were truly concerned about the housing needs of Canadians they would accept and act on the Liberal amendments. If they do not, it will further confirm to Canadians that the Conservatives should not have a mandate to govern, a conclusion Canadians
December 4, 1979

have already reached according to the Gallup poll after putting up with this non-government for only six months.

Members of the New Democratic Party are going to vote against this bill because we feel it will give assistance to those who need it the least while ignoring completely the problems of those really in need.
This is a government which railed against the deficits of the former government and said it would reduce those deficits.
